# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

screens.why4: The rows are distinct and in my words, but the card's fixed 'Nobody else' first row is not shown, so I can't see that option on the list.
screens.why5: It keeps exactly my two roles, The CFO and The project executive, in my order, adds no role I never named, and keeps the superintendent and the operations lead apart as I said.
screens.why7: Every row is tagged, there are at most two 'has to agree' roles, both in my words and order, and none was dropped or invented, but the fixed 'Nobody else' first row the card's shape requires is missing from the list.
screens.instead: Show 'Nobody else · does not have to agree' as the fixed first row above the same four rows, so the list has the shape the card asks for.

screens.why1: Right after I named the CFO and the project executive as the people who have to agree, it makes sense to ask which version of the belief I want to test.
screens.why2: The two rows are plain, but the bar's 'the last time they paid for something for this' is vague and took me a second read, since my buyers would be asked whether they could sign off on $1k a month, not about a past purchase.
screens.why3: I know who has to bless a per-site software spend at a GC, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: The card asks for two rows here, Nobody else first and then my roles tagged 'has to agree', and the screen shows exactly that, in my words, distinct and complete.
screens.why5: Both roles I typed, the CFO and the project executive, are kept in my order and joined with 'and', and the contractor operations lead stays the decider.
screens.why7: The roles, the order and the belief all meet the card, but the bar breaks two of its rules: it uses the past-purchase wording ('the last time they paid') where the decision-maker's link asks 'Could you sign off on it yourself', and it counts only 'had to agree' as support, leaving out 'I could sign off myself', which the card also counts for.
screens.instead: Bar: Holds if at least 2 in 3 contractor operations leads say they could sign off on about $1k a site a month themselves, or that the CFO would have to agree.

screens.why1: Right after who has to agree, asking what the contractor's side has to clear before paying is the obvious next step in how a site subscription sells.
screens.why2: "What must the buyer's own side clear before they pay" is plain to me, and the hint's example and its "not your own trial or pilot" tell me exactly what kind of row to type.
screens.why3: I've been through these with the GCs we've pitched: their ops and IT people want to know it works with Procore and what happens to the site videos, so I answer from what I've seen.
screens.why4: The only option is a box for my own steps plus the single escape "Leave this out of the study", which is the right founder-side escape for this dimension.
screens.why5: What's typed is my two steps in my words, "A check that it works with Procore; A security review of the site videos", with nothing added or reworded.
screens.why7: Both rows are brakes on the contractor's side, each a noun phrase with its object under 9 words, neither is my trial or pilot nor overlaps the other, the time is left for me to type next, and the escape is there.

screens.why1: Right after I named who decides and who signs off, it makes sense to check the steps a GC's side has to clear before paying per site.
screens.why2: The rows are in my words, but the line under the list saying 'Keel's draft broke one of its own rules' doesn't say which rule or which row, so I'd read it twice and still not know what to fix.
screens.why3: I sell to GCs and know they'll ask whether it pushes into Procore and what happens to video of their sites, so I can answer from my own sales calls.
screens.why4: 'An IT review of new software' overlaps 'A security review of the site videos': at most GCs that security review is the IT review, so two rows mean nearly the same brake.
screens.why5: My Procore check and my security review are kept in my words, but my trial on one live job is gone (rightly, it's my own offer), and the Procore row drops ACC, which half my segment runs on.
screens.why7: Every row is a buyer-side brake I don't control, and the founder's own trial is out, but Keel's added row is a generic formality that contains the security review rather than a separate gate this GC's process has, so the no-overlap rule is bent.
screens.instead: What has to happen first: A check that it works with Procore or ACC · A security review of the site videos (drop 'An IT review of new software', or name the real extra gate, e.g. the owner's sign-off on filming their site).

screens.why1: Right after I listed what the GC's side has to clear, picking one step and putting my own time on it is the obvious next move before the buyer questions.
screens.why2: Procore check, security review of the site videos, IT review: these are the words an ops lead at a GC and I both use, and the intro and time box read cleanly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know from selling to GCs which of these holds a deal up and roughly how long a Procore integration check takes, so I can pick and put a number on it from my own pipeline.
screens.why4: The third row, an IT review of new software, mostly contains the security review of the site videos, since at most GCs the security look happens inside the IT review, so two rows overlap.
screens.why5: My two steps are kept in my words, the pick is the Procore check I meant, and the 2 weeks in the belief is the time I typed.
screens.why7: Measure, pick, founder-typed time, the 2-in-3 bar and the I'm-not-sure escape all fit the card, but Keel's added row is a generic formality that contains my security-review row rather than a separate gate this buyer has, and it is not marked as suggested.
screens.instead: Same screen with only my two steps, 'A check that it works with Procore' and 'A security review of the site videos', or, if Keel must add one, a GC-specific gate such as 'The owner's sign-off on recording the site', tagged suggested; time box empty for my 2 weeks; I'm not sure.

screens.why1: After who decides, the price and what the buyer's side must clear, asking for the first step I want the contractor to take is the obvious last commercial question (6 of 6).
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but the question asks two things ('the step' and 'what would it cost them') into one box, so I read it twice before seeing that the hint wants the cost folded into the step ('where any money goes').
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask a GC to do first: put us on one live job for a paid month.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip 'Leave this out of the study', which correctly leaves the dimension out the way the card's 'I'm not sure' does.
screens.why5: My answer 'start a paid pilot on one site' stands as I typed it, with the contractor operations lead named as the one who takes it.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step of at most 9 words that the buyer takes, naming where the money goes, which fits the founder's one_step shape; 'start a paid pilot on one site' fits it, and the cost cue sets up the free smaller step; the escape is allowed on the founder's side.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the contractor operations lead to take? (One step, up to 9 words; say if it costs them money, e.g. "start a paid pilot on one site" or "let us film one site walk".)

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, Keel shows me how strangers will hear it, and that is the natural check before Part 3's last item.
screens.why2: 'Start a paid pilot on one site' is how a GC talks about trying software on a job, and the belief and bar read cleanly on first pass.
screens.why3: Whether an ops lead at a GC would put one live job on a paid pilot is exactly the call I make with my buyers every week.
screens.why4: The two rows show only their word counts (7/9 and 8/9) and not the step and smaller step themselves or the four answers the ops lead will see, so I'm checking a box I can't fully read.
screens.why5: The step is mine word for word, 'paid pilot on one site' with the money and the single site kept, and the decider is the contractor operations lead I named.
screens.why7: The step costs money, so a second, free smaller-step row sits under it within 9 words; the belief 'In most cases the contractor operations lead would start a paid pilot on one site' is the step itself; and with the card's fixed four (yes / probably after the smaller step / probably not / no), no escape and a 1-in-3 bar, it can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Show the rows' text beside their counts: 'start a paid pilot on one site' (7/9) and the free smaller step (8/9), then the four answers: Yes, I'd start a paid pilot on one site · Probably, after {smaller step} first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right place to decide whether strangers get asked to try Fresco for real, and it follows straight on from the Commitment step I just set.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot, the email line and the Pilot tab are all plain to me as a founder; I answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my own call, and I know I do: I'm asking for introductions to commercial GCs.
screens.why4: Yes or No is the whole choice, the two are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: My step was 'start a paid pilot on one site', bought by the contractor, but the line strangers see is a free-sounding 'try this for real, leave your email', and it doesn't say whether it goes to the supers who use it or the operations leads who pay, so the paid, per-site meaning has drifted.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Strangers who say yes see: 'Would you start a paid pilot on one site? Leave your email.' (shown to: Contractor operations leads / Superintendents / Both) -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my supers the questions belongs right before the link goes out, after the pilot offer and before the last check.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint crams video, voice, the typing fallback, one-time recording, credits and the text link into one block, and 'records the voice once' and '400 credits' need a second read.
screens.why3: Picking how the interviewer sounds to a superintendent on a jobsite is a call I can make by listening to two five-second clips.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a preview, the default is marked, and the cost is the same either way, so nothing is missing and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: Nothing about Fresco or my buyer roles changes or leaks; it only names construction superintendents and keeps the text-message link they would actually open.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions? Hear each voice, then pick one. (Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s). Put the cost (400 credits either way) and 'they can read and type instead' on a short second line.

screens.why1: Screen 23 set how superintendents are asked, so asking next how the buyer side answers its own link belongs here, just before sending.
screens.why2: Video with an interviewer, read and tap, or let them pick are plain choices to me, and each option says in one line what the respondent does.
screens.why3: I know how my general-contractor contacts take a link: ops leads on a phone or laptop between meetings, so I can judge read-and-tap against a video interviewer.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete (one mode, the other, or both), and none is odd or missing.
screens.why5: I typed the buyer as the contractor's operations lead, and 'contractors' blurs that into the firm, so it no longer says plainly that this is the buyer link and not the superintendents' link.
screens.instead: How should contractor operations leads answer the buyer questions? (AI interviewer · Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: After choosing how contractors answer, the last step is deciding who receives the interview links, so the question lands exactly where I'd expect it.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'the Contacts page' and 'From a search' assume I know a Keel feature never shown in the flow, so the second option needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to supers and ops leads I've met through intros or posting in a group, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three options cover named contacts, a Keel-sourced list and an open group link, they don't overlap, and my pick 'People I know by name' is there.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed, and none of my product or roles leaks to the people I'll send to.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (one link each) / A list Keel found for me (one link each, I send them) / A group, with one open link I post where they are

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title with its deciding number, 'Price: 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month', but I have to wonder why Price leads when Purchase friction and Commitment are marked the harsher-sounding 'Did not hold'.
screens.why_b2: Most count lines read straight off as 'k of n · bar', but the kicker's '1 TO 8 COUNTED', Existing sacrifice being over 7 not 8, and Ability to pay's '5 needed' (5 of what?) each take a second look.
screens.why_b3: The six names and belief lines are mine: 30 to 60 hours per site a month, $800 to $1,000, the operations lead with the CFO and project executive, the Procore check within 2 weeks, a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: the line under the verdict only says who was asked, not whether to drop the price toward what the 7 named, make the pilot cheaper, or pre-clear the Procore check.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the 5-of-7 hours belief is only called 'at the bar', but two status words ('Not holding up' vs 'Did not hold') are never told apart, so Purchase friction at 1 short reads as final as Price at 1 of 8.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: 1 of 8 contractor operations leads would pay $800 or more per site a month, though 5 of 7 put the hours it saves at 30 or more; test a lower price or a cheaper first-site pilot before anything else.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 spend 30 hours or more per site a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip says it counts hours of the daily log per site a month, one cell per person over 7 counted, and marks my bar at 5 of 7, so I get all three on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Existing sacrifice and the belief line uses my 30 to 60 hours per site a month, but it drops 'on commercial jobs' from the people I named, so it is recognisably mine but not word for word.
screens.why_b4: The So line just points me to the Price card, which I already read as not holding up, instead of saying what matters: 40 hours a site at $55 is about $2,200 a month against my $800-1,000, so the buyers carry the cost but won't pay my price, which means I should sell on the hours they already spend.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n in view and calls it 'a lean, not a call', but the So line says flatly 'The cost is there' for a result sitting exactly at the bar on 7 people, and Trevor's '10.9 hours' looks like a dollar amount converted to hours with no explanation.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 operations leads put the daily log at 30 hours or more per site a month (median 40, roughly $2,200 at $55 an hour), above your $800-1,000 price, yet only 1 of 8 would pay it; on 7 people this is a lean, so the next step is to pitch the hours you give back, not the software.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each buyer's monthly per-site band over 8 people, marks where my $800 to $1,000 sits, and the strip shows 1 for against 7 against with the marker at 6, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Price and the belief is exactly mine: contractor operations leads would think Fresco worth $800 to $1,000 per site a month.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and sends me to the Insights tab, but it doesn't say what this means for Fresco, such as that 5 of 8 sit under $500 while the existing-sacrifice card says supers spend about 40 hours a site a month, so the gap is in what the buyer believes they pay, not in the cost itself.
screens.why_b5: n stays at 8, the small group is called a lean not a call, and nothing is claimed beyond the eight buyers who answered.
screens.instead: 7 of 8 buyers put Fresco under $800 a site, 5 of them under $500, yet supers spend about 40 hours a site a month on logs; show buyers those hours, or test a lower per-site price or a free one-job pilot, before holding at $1k.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know the belief is unread and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where the money would come from for the one contractor asked, but the strip's '4 of 5' bar with four ghost cells beside a single real answer takes a second look to see it is the 5-person floor, not five people who answered.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay is named, and the line uses my buyer (contractor operations leads) and my $800 to $1,000 per site a month price, so it reads as my own pricing belief even though Keel derived it rather than me typing it.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' is generic, and it never says the real point: this waits on Price, which failed at 1 of 8, and Gordon, the one contractor who reached my price, needs a new budget line signed off.
screens.why_b5: With one person, 'a lean, not a call' still hints at a direction, and 'said where the money would come from' sounds favourable when Gordon's answer counts against; the rule line's 'or none' names an answer that is not on the chart, and it leaves out charged to sites and outside funding.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon reached $800, and his money would need a new budget line, which counts against. Ability to pay can't be read until Price holds, so fix the price or the pitch to the CFO first.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, marked 'at the bar', so I know it held and by how little.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to the sign-off question across all 8 who answered, and the strip puts the marker at 6 of 8 (at least 2 in 3), so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief line is mine word for word: the operations lead decides, and the CFO and the project executive must agree; the item testing only the CFO is the registry's open choice, not a fault of this screen.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the CFO in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone' tells me concretely to build the pilot pitch around getting the CFO's sign-off, while knowing a couple of ops leads may just sign.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ('a small group: a lean, not a call') and the result is held only at the bar, but 'the CFO in most deals' overreaches slightly when only 4 of 8 actually named the CFO and 2 more said it was wider than that.
screens.instead: Plan for the CFO: 4 of 8 said the CFO would have to agree, 2 said it was wider than that, and 2 could sign alone. This held at the bar, so treat it as a lean.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "5 of 8 under 2 weeks or not needed · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short", so I know the verdict and the one person it missed by.
screens.why_b2: The bands are labelled for or against with their counts, the 8 people are in the strip and the marker sits at 6, and the chart says outright that my 2 weeks is the low edge of the first band against.
screens.why_b3: It is my Procore check and my 2 weeks, put to contractor operations leads, worded a little longer ("a check that it works with Procore") but plainly mine.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of that length" gives me a duration, but it doesn't say that all three against sit in the band just past my 2 weeks, so making the Procore check shorter up front (a demo push to their Procore project) would likely flip it.
screens.why_b5: n stays at 8, the count line calls it "a lean, not a call", and the card says the band starting at my own 2 weeks counts against, so nothing claims more than eight people can carry.
screens.instead: All 3 who expect longer chose 2 weeks to 1 month, none longer: the Procore check runs just past your 2 weeks rather than far past it, so either plan on about a month or cut the check down by showing the Procore push before they buy.

screens.why_b1: Did not hold sits right beside 3 of 8 said yes against a bar of 6 of 8, 3 short, so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: What is counted, the 8 people and the bar at 6 are plain, but the soft yes reads 'a free look at it first' in the chart and 'a free look at it on sample data first' in the rule line, so I had to look twice to be sure it was the same answer that got zero.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'start a paid pilot on one site' with my operations lead as the decider is the belief I checked, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats that 5 of 8 would not and sends me to the Insights tab; it does not say the concrete thing, that a paid pilot is too big a first step for most leads and I should open with something smaller.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, everyone is counted and named, and the small group is called a lean, not a call, so nothing claims more than the answers carry.
screens.instead: Word the soft yes the same in the rule line and the chart, drop the doubled Asked and the repeated 'if it were offered today', and have the So line say no one took the free look either, so a paid pilot as the first step lost 5 of 8 leads and I should test a cheaper first step.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding count beside it: Price not holding at 1 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction 5 of 8 and 1 short, Commitment 3 of 8 and 3 short.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are my dimensions, and the belief lines are the ones I set: $800 to $1,000 per site a month, the Procore check within about 2 weeks, and a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: The Price quotes point to moves (price per active super, show the firm the hours first, a free first month), but the screen never says what the failures mean for the idea, and the two empty boxes give me nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: No count is overstated and n stays visible, but 'never saw it (Sandra, Omar, Trevor)' on Commitment, for people who answered and are quoted on Price, reads as if they skipped the question when they were only not asked the why.
screens.why_b6: The Price quotes tell me things I didn't type: buyers can't put a figure on log time, supers' unpaid evenings aren't a cost the firm counts, a second per-site fee on top of Procore stings, pricing per active super would go higher, and buyers fear the liability of an AI-written legal record.
screens.instead: Price fails mostly because operations leads can't see what the logs cost them and balk at a per-site fee on top of Procore: lead with measured hours, test per-super pricing or a free first month on one job, and note that nobody was asked why on Purchase friction or Commitment.

screens.why1: This is the first screen of my link and I'm the one who'd pay, so showing me the idea before any buying questions is the obvious place to start.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, Procore, ACC, action items, assignees are all words I use every week, and "AI scribe" is explained in the same sentence.
screens.why3: I know how my supers run their walks and what ends up in Procore, so I can picture this on my jobs without guessing.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The founder's moment is after the walks, when the photos and notes still have to get into the daily log, but the card says "notes" not the daily log and puts it "during your site walk", which isn't mine to walk, it's my supers'.
screens.why6: It's one idea said cleanly, but the "how" runs four sentences where the card should be three lines, and "notes with photos, assignees and due dates" is a lot to hold heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an AI scribe for site walks. Your superintendents talk over short videos on the walk, and it writes up the daily log with photos, action items and due dates, then sends it to Procore or ACC. The people building it believe your supers would use it at the end of the day, once the walks are done and the log still has to be written.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and opening the buying part, asking what the daily log already costs us in hours is the obvious first thing before any talk of price.
screens.why2: Daily log, hours per site, last month: these are plain words in my trade, and I'd answer them on first hearing.
screens.why3: I pay for the tools and know roughly what my supers put into the daily log, but I don't track their log hours per site, so I'd be estimating from what they tell me.
screens.why4: An open box for hours, None as zero, and I can't recall as the single escape cover every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: It asks about the daily log in our own words, and nothing of the product or the founder's terms comes through.
screens.why6: It's one short question with a clear unit and one escape, and I'd answer it after hearing it once, though the spoken line 'A number of hours per site last month' is a slightly stiff fragment.
screens.why7: The box asks the founder's own unit, base and period (hours per site a month), so any answer sits above or below 30, and the one escape, I can't recall, is there, matching the card's good example.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours spent on the daily log, asking what it is worth a month per site is the obvious next question for the person who pays.
screens.why2: A monthly fee per site is how we already buy job-site software, so the stem and the dollar bands read plainly on first pass.
screens.why3: I sign off on per-site subscriptions like Procore add-ons, so I can say what this would be worth from what I actually pay.
screens.why4: Five non-overlapping dollar bands plus a clean 'I wouldn't pay for this' cover every answer, and 'I can't say' sits apart as the one escape.
screens.why5: The card names the product on purpose and the stem carries the founder's per-site monthly unit with no leaning word, so nothing leaks beyond the idea card.
screens.why6: Spoken in two steps of four then two short options, with the one escape said last as 'Or say: I can't say,' it is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: One measure (dollars per site a month), six rungs with a band edge exactly at the founder's $800 low, two bands plus would-not-pay against and three bands for, and the cant_say escape present and alone.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next thing to ask the person who signs for the software.
screens.why2: It reads my pick back the way I'd say it, about $500 to $800 a site a month, and asks a plain question I can answer straight off.
screens.why3: I know what would make a daily-log tool worth more to me, like whether it pushes clean into Procore, saves my supers real hours, and holds up in a claim, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It names Fresco, which the idea card already showed me on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, and the dollar range says cleanly aloud.

screens.why1: Right after I put a number on it, asking whether I could approve that spend myself or need sign-off is the obvious next thing a vendor would want to know.
screens.why2: Sign off, CFO and per site a month are how we talk about software spend at a GC, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I approve and pay for the tools our job sites run on, so I know exactly where my signing limit sits and when finance has to get involved.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to it not being my call, the CFO row is named, and I can't say is a fair way out; if it were our owner or president instead of the CFO I'd still have Several people or someone else's call.
screens.why5: Nothing reads like a pitch; it names the price and one role a GC would plausibly have, and the CFO reads as the founder's own pick, kept as typed.
screens.why6: One short either-or question, a dollar figure that says easily, and four short answers plus the escape that I can hold after one hearing.
screens.why7: One measure (who has to agree), the four in order from alone to someone else's call with the CFO named second, I can't say set apart, and two answers count for and two against.

screens.why1: Right after asking who signs off on the money, asking what else stands between me and buying it is the obvious next step for someone in my seat.
screens.why2: A check that it works with Procore is exactly how I'd say it, because every new tool on our jobs has to play with Procore before I'll pay for it.
screens.why3: I'm the one who gets a new app vetted against our Procore setup with our admin and IT, so I know roughly how long that takes us.
screens.why4: The bands run end to end with no gaps or overlaps, 'It wouldn't be needed' covers a tool already in the Procore marketplace that we've used, and 'I can't tell' fits a purchase I haven't made.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or roles comes through, just a plain step in my words with Procore, the tool my jobs actually run on.
screens.why6: One short question, four options I can hold, the escape said last, and a two-option follow-up, so I could answer it on the first hearing.
screens.why7: Every option measures one thing, how long the step takes; the bands are five with an edge at 2 weeks and 'It wouldn't be needed' last; both sides can win; and 'I can't tell' is the one escape the card requires.

screens.why1: After the price, who signs off, and the Procore check, the last buying question is whether I'd actually put it on a job, so it lands right where I'd expect it.
